James. The Hitchcock material is Johnson’s view of her grandmother’s experience; the underlying account is Tippi Hedren’s, and Vanity Fair supplies the characterization of Hitchcock’s conduct. claims.claim: Interpretation: the Six case (anxiety, vigilance, loyalty, ambivalence toward authority, trusted guide) is why confidence is medium.
claims.passage: The Six reading is not refuted, only outweighed on content. Hence medium confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes C20, C22, C29, C45, C90, C91, C100 and C181.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the discriminator between Four and Six is the relation between her fear and her grievance, stated as this profile’s reading of the interviews reviewed (2015–2026). Every fear she names in this record is circumstantial (fame, not working, the contract at 23, singing, directing, press scrutiny). The test for a Six is whether fear and grievance fuse in one figure: an authority who misled her, left her exposed, or imposed its will without the right to; the Four’s grievance is the loss of what was true in the work.
claims.passage: Here is the test this profile rests on, stated as a reading, not a fact about her. Every fear she names in this record is circumstantial: fame (2015, 2017), not working (2016), a contract at 23 (2022), singing (2021), directing (2025), press scrutiny (2026). The test for a Six is whether fear and grievance fuse in one figure: an authority who misled her, left her exposed, or imposed its will on her without the right to.
claims.inference: Scoped to the reviewed record and marked as the profile’s reading (subject-01, future-01). The Six side of the test now includes an authority resisted as illegitimate, not only betrayal (enneagram-03). The passage no longer claims she “never” described being misled or unprotected; the protection-shaped lines in the record (C100, C26, C181, C179, C79) are quoted and weighed in C222 and C210.
claims.alternative: Her incentive to protect working relationships (“I don’t want to hurt anyone’s career”) could be suppressing a trust grievance; the record was not exhausted (Good Hang with Amy Poehler, June 10, 2025, unopened).
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if she describes any production conflict as being misled or left unprotected, or if a collaborator describes her complaint that way.

claims.claim: Recalling learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny didn’t exist, she said in 2022, “But if I could, I would still believe in it now. Maybe that’s why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe.”
claims.passage: Recalling the morning at 10 when she learned the Easter Bunny was not real, she said in 2022, "But if I could, I would still believe in it now. Maybe that's why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe."
claims.inference: In this line belief and moviemaking serve safety; the edit stage moved it from the Four side to the Six case.
claims.alternative: A light anecdote about enchantment; a Four could also treat make-believe as refuge.

claims.claim: She said of choosing projects in 2020, “I really don’t have a method, and I don’t want one… It’s very intuitive and emotional.”
claims.passage: "I really don't have a method, and I don't want one" (2020)
claims.inference: Resistance to method; the article now counts it as consistent with the counterphobic Six as well as the Four rather than against Six (enneagram-02).
claims.alternative: A Seven or Nine could also resist method; producers often say this in interviews.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I think I just find rules and some structure really ridiculous, silly and stupid,” and told Vogue in 2026, “Rules are really tough for me.”
claims.passage: rules "really ridiculous, silly and stupid" (2024) and "really tough for me" (2026)
claims.inference: Resistance to rules corroborated across two outlets and years; counted as consistent with the counterphobic Six as well as the Four (enneagram-02).
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Six (reflexive defiance of authority), Eight (autonomy) and Nine (accommodate, then quietly do your own thing) all fit parts of this.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring.”
claims.passage: Decision-makers "want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring,"
claims.inference: She disdains safety-seeking and control in creative decisions, the opposite of what a security-first motive would defend.
claims.alternative: Common artist rhetoric during a bad box-office moment; also fits Eight anti-control sentiment.

claims.claim: She has said she has struggled with depression “since I was 15 or 14” and “I am in a lot of therapy” (Marie Claire, 2020), adding, “But I’ve learned to find it beautiful because I feel the world”; she is “always trying to navigate that in an honest and safe way” (Vanity Fair, 2022); Vogue (2026) reports various modalities of therapy; she received the Hope for Depression Research Foundation’s HOPE Award in November 2023.
claims.passage: Her depression, which she dates to "15 or 14," and the therapy she credits
claims.inference: First-person mental-health history with the professional and personal support she credits in all three sources. Not used as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Depression can mimic Four melancholy; the article states it is not type evidence (C154). Wikipedia’s unsourced rehabilitation claim is not used.

claims.claim: She said she felt like her Lost Daughter character, Nina, “so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach,” adding, “I feel like that in my career a lot” (2021).
claims.passage: She felt like her _Lost Daughter_ character, "so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach,"
claims.inference: Names being seen accurately, beyond surface image, as a career-long hunger and as the basis of trust.
claims.alternative: Awards-campaign talk about a role; actors routinely identify with characters. The specificity (“the hot girl on the beach,” trust built on not being seen) is the evidence.

claims.claim: She said she trusted Gyllenhaal “because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen. She knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care” (2021).
claims.passage: She trusted Gyllenhaal "because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen. She knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care" (2021)
claims.inference: Two grounds for the trust, one about being seen (Four vocabulary) and one about care and handling (Six vocabulary); the article quotes both and no longer says the trust “rested on being seen” (fan-03, critic-02).
claims.alternative: The care clause is protection language a Six reading can claim; weighed in C222.

claims.claim: Richard E. Grant said in 2022 that “having seen her on that infamous Ellen DeGeneres interview, you know that she takes no prisoners.”
claims.passage: Richard E. Grant, her _Persuasion_ costar, to say in 2022, "you know that she takes no prisoners."
claims.inference: A forceful public presence, partly derived from the Ellen clip (Grant says so).
claims.alternative: Fits Eight; much of it is costar warmth in promotional contexts.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said that after two years of exposure she went into “this weird K-hole of feeling so scared of people” and became “shut off to strangers, even cold. That’s not my nature. I prefer to be tender”; Vogue reported in 2017 that tender is her favorite word and tattooed on her forearm.
claims.passage: "I think I went into this weird K-hole of feeling so scared of people. I noticed myself becoming shut off to strangers, even cold. That's not my nature. I prefer to be tender."
claims.inference: Volunteered vulnerability, with the fear clause restored at the edit stage; dated to 2017.
claims.alternative: Fear of people also feeds the Six case; an Eight can admit softness privately, but these are public admissions.

claims.claim: She said in September 2018, at the Venice press conference for Suspiria as reported by Entertainment Weekly, “I’m a very porous person and I absorb a lot of people’s feelings.”
claims.passage: she calls herself "a very porous person" who absorbs "a lot of people's feelings"
claims.inference: Volunteered permeability, repeated as “porous” in 2026.
claims.alternative: A press-conference remark walking back an earlier Elle report; first read through JoBlo’s relay, now checked against the EW original’s Wayback capture (verify-06).

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I can be out at my house and not see or speak to another human for days on end, and I feel wonderful.”
claims.passage: "I can be out at my house and not see or speak to another human for days on end, and I feel wonderful," she said in 2024.
claims.inference: Withdrawal and rest are restorative for her.
claims.alternative: Strongest support for a Nine or withdrawn reading; depression and exhausting schedules also explain it.

claims.claim: On Madame Web she was “just sort of along for the ride” (2025).
claims.passage: On _Madame Web_ she was "along for the ride."
claims.inference: Nine-like passivity in one project.
claims.alternative: Could be resignation on a studio film.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said, “I think I’m a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I’m in a happy relationship. I don’t do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt.”
claims.passage: "I think I'm a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I'm in a happy relationship. I don't do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt."
claims.inference: Longing and heightened feeling as a standing condition rather than a reaction to events, stated nine years apart.
claims.alternative: Depression (C04) and an actor’s trained emotional access can produce the same language.

claims.claim: Her friend Talia Bernstein says, “She’s sillier than most people know… I’ve been at so many small gatherings with her where she’s putting on a dance or changing into a costume…. She likes to laugh” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: "She's sillier than most people know," her friend Talia Bernstein told Vogue in 2026, describing gatherings where "she's putting on a dance or changing into a costume."
claims.inference: A strong playful, mischievous streak that coexists with the melancholy self-description.
claims.alternative: Fits Seven; the melancholy-only Four stereotype does not predict it.

claims.claim: Asked about motherhood in 2024, she said, “I really want to experience everything that life has to offer,” and a few sentences later, “There’s so much to eat up and learn and grow from and experience and feel. That includes all the pain and the suffering and feeling so helpless about the world.”
claims.passage: Asked about motherhood in 2024, she said, "I really want to experience everything that life has to offer," close to a Seven's motto. A few sentences later: "That includes all the pain and the suffering and feeling so helpless about the world."
claims.inference: Unlike a Seven’s appetite, hers explicitly embraces suffering and self-reproach as part of what she wants to feel.
claims.alternative: Read alone, “experience everything” is Seven language; the second half is what separates it.

claims.claim: She said in 2017, “The stories I want to tell, the characters I want to play, don’t typically exist in huge, commercial box-office movies… But this is a business.”
claims.passage: the stories she wants to tell "don't typically exist in huge, commercial box-office movies," she said in 2017. "But this is a business."
claims.inference: Commercial calculation that supports a Three reading; the same sentence names non-commercial taste.
claims.alternative: Supports a Three or practical-careerist reading of some choices; tempers the purist image.

claims.claim: In March 2024 she said she probably would never do anything like Madame Web again; in June 2025, “There’s no part of me that’s like, ‘Oh, I’ll never do that again’ to anything. I’ve done even tiny movies that didn’t do well. Who cares?”
claims.passage: and the vow was gone: "There's no part of me that's like, 'Oh, I'll never do that again' to anything. I've done even tiny movies that didn't do well. Who cares?"
claims.inference: Stated plans change with the moment; the shrug at films that “didn’t do well” cuts against an image-protecting Three reading (C155) and against reputational distancing as the whole story (C140).
claims.alternative: Press context or a joke.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her anxiety is high for a Four, and depression can mimic Four melancholy.
claims.passage: The fear is loud for a Four. Anxiety and self-doubt run through every decade of her record, and the depression she describes can resemble Four melancholy without being a personality trait
claims.inference: Counterevidence and a diagnosis-vs-personality caution. The clause that followed (a Four with a Six’s cover and a Six with a Four’s cover “can be told apart only by content, never by temperature”) restated the test section’s content-versus-temperature test and was cut on repair for length (verify-07).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Sources from outside her promotional circle are Sam Taylor-Johnson (S35), E.L. James (S44), The Ringer (S38) and two February 2024 critics’ essays (S51, S52); none is a collaborator’s critical account of her as a producer, and none speaks to her private motives.
claims.passage: Almost every voice here is a friend or collaborator in a promotional piece; Taylor-Johnson and James are the only outside voices quoted, and neither speaks to her motives. No critical first-hand account of her as a producer has surfaced.
claims.inference: Source-limit statement.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if a collaborator, crew member or financier gives a critical first-hand account of a TeaTime production or of her conduct on set.

claims.claim: The July 2026 Vogue interview was timed to Verity, a thriller costarring Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett; the film opened in North America on the weekend of October 2–4, 2026 and took in $32.6 million in its first weekend (AFP, citing Exhibitor Relations) despite weak reviews; Johnson was 36.
claims.passage: for Vogue's October cover timed to the thriller _Verity_, which opened that October
claims.inference: Dated context only; not needed for the argument.
claims.alternative: Release details shift.
claims.review_trigger: Update the gross only if the article cites it; the first-weekend figure is an initial industry report and final totals may differ.

claims.claim: Vogue reports that when filming ends on a project with “this really intense connection to the material” and everyone goes home, she finds it “shattering,” and she said, “I’ve felt that sort of heartbreak I don’t even know how many times now in my life… It’s like leaving summer camp. It’s so devastating. And I don’t know how much more heartbreak my heart can handle.”
claims.passage: "I've felt that sort of heartbreak I don't even know how many times now in my life," she said. "It's like leaving summer camp. It's so devastating. And I don't know how much more heartbreak my heart can handle."
claims.inference: Intense, recurring grief at the end of a shoot she is deeply connected to (Vogue’s condition, kept at the repair stage); she presents it as a thing that happens on set, not as unique to her.
claims.alternative: Common among actors; depression also colors it.

claims.claim: Vogue says the Stromboli shoot was the kind of thing she joined the industry to be part of: “a safe container full of artists feeling free.”
claims.passage: The set Vogue says she joined the industry for is "a safe container full of artists feeling free,"
claims.inference: Vogue’s phrase, attributed as such.
claims.alternative: The writer’s framing.

claims.claim: Interpretation: wrap grief is common and a Six could mourn a lost secure group; what is specific is how often she says it recurs and what ends.
claims.passage: Plenty of actors grieve a wrap, and a Six could mourn the loss of a secure group.
claims.inference: Replaces the draft’s unsupported “most actors” contrast.
claims.alternative: Actors commonly grieve wrap; the Six reading of a lost secure group is stated in the passage.

claims.claim: In the same Bustle interview she said, “Truly, but I know I’ve exaggerated in this interview, and you can tell that I’m exaggerating because you see my face. If it’s written down, it’s hard.”
claims.passage: She also warned that she had "exaggerated in this interview," so every Bustle line here carries that caveat.
claims.inference: Discloses her own caveat where Bustle lines first carry weight; no discriminator rests on a single Bustle line without corroboration.
claims.alternative: The caveat may itself be a joke; it applies to tone, not to every line.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the 2017 and 2018 Fifty Shades praise dates from the years she later said she could not talk about truthfully.
claims.passage: The first thing to know about the fight is how long she declined to describe it.
claims.inference: Flags that “different is what I’m about” is a promotional-period line.
claims.alternative: The praise may have been sincere; see C148.

claims.claim: Asked about regret in 2022, she said, “If I had known at the time that’s what it was going to be like, I don’t think anyone would’ve done it. It would’ve been like, ‘Oh, this is psychotic.’ But no, I don’t regret it.”
claims.passage: On regret: "If I had known at the time that's what it was going to be like, I don't think anyone would've done it. It would've been like, 'Oh, this is psychotic.' But no, I don't regret it."
claims.inference: The conditional is restored so “psychotic” reads as a hypothetical reaction with foreknowledge, not her verdict on the finished experience (subject-07, fan-07, critic-01).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Madame Web, a superhero film, opened in February 2024 to poor reviews and weak box office: Bustle’s March 2024 question concerned its “nasty reviews,” the Los Angeles Times (June 2025) called it “a box-office bomb,” and Wikipedia describes it as critically and commercially unsuccessful.
claims.passage: In February 2024 the superhero film _Madame Web_ opened to poor reviews and weak box office.
claims.inference: Orients readers to the film and its reception in neutral prose; the live-wiki quotation was replaced with dated contemporaneous sources (future-04).
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the timing of her 2022 Fifty Shades account (four years after the trilogy’s last film in 2018 and a year after The Lost Daughter in 2021) fits reputational distancing, and the article says so in the Three section.
claims.passage: her 2022 account came four years after the franchise ended and a year after _The Lost Daughter_, when distancing cost least.
claims.inference: Names and tests the reputational-distancing alternative with the timing stated (critic-05); the counterweights are the billion-dollar franchise, the shrug at flops and grievances aimed at contrivance rather than reception (C155).
claims.alternative: Fifty Shades was critically mocked, so distancing from it remains possible; a Three reading is conceded as not cleanly separable (C229).

claims.claim: L’Officiel (2024) says the Ellen interview “set the internet on fire in 2019”; Vogue (2026) dates her deadpan press reputation to the Ellen clip and the AD video.
claims.passage: L'Officiel dates the viral version of it to 2019
claims.inference: Dates the viral persona so readers can check that the 2017 put-on and Foley’s 2017 remark come before it.
claims.alternative: The Ringer traces press-junket mischief to 2015; the viral reputation is what dates to 2019.

claims.claim: In the same Ellen exchange, after recalling being teased about it on the show the year before, Johnson said, “But I did invite you, and you didn’t come,” and DeGeneres conceded, “No, I think I do remember I was invited.”
claims.passage: She added, "But I did invite you, and you didn't come," and DeGeneres conceded, "No, I think I do remember I was invited."
claims.inference: Context from the same transcript for why she pushed back.
claims.alternative: Captions are unlabeled; attribution rests on sequence (“you gave me a bunch of [BLEEP] about not inviting you. But I did invite you”) and contemporaneous descriptions.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the pride she stated during promotion (2016, 2017, 2018) is the pride she repeated in 2022 (“I’m proud of what we made ultimately”); what she withheld until 2022 was the fight, not her feeling about the result.
claims.passage: What she withheld was the fight.
claims.inference: Weighs C67 against C08 and C171 (and the 2018 Flicks defense, S11, not quoted): the 2017 answers admit recurring regret (“It comes in waves”) and state pride; the 2022 account adds the fight.
claims.alternative: A Three or a loyal Six would also hold a promotional line; the reading is inference from her later account, and Marie Claire’s undated note of a denial (S07) has no wording to check beyond the 2017 statements (C156).

claims.claim: Interpretation: protection from collaborators, then the freedom to act, is the shape Six theory predicts.
claims.passage: Protection from trusted collaborators, then the freedom to act, is the shape Six theory predicts.
claims.inference: Concedes that the safety framing does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: A Four needs safety too.

claims.claim: Interpretation: on her talk of safety alone, the Six reading would win.
claims.passage: Still, on her talk of fear and safety alone, the Six reading would win.
claims.inference: States plainly that the Four lead rests on the grievance and being-seen evidence (C95, C16, C100).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her depression and therapy are care for a medical condition and are not used as type evidence.
claims.passage: are a medical matter and are not counted for any type.
claims.inference: Implements the standard’s caution against treating a mood disorder as personality.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Three reading has support (commercial frankness, years on message, the timing of the 2022 account, self-deprecation as image management, “It wasn’t my fault”), but she shrugs at flops, says she doesn’t “make sense” in the superhero world, would accept Three Incestuous Sisters as her last film, and aims her grievances at contrivance rather than reception.
claims.passage: Against that, she shrugs at "tiny movies that didn't do well," says she doesn't "make sense" in the superhero world, would accept the Rohrwacher film as her last, and aims a decade of grievances at contrivance rather than at reception.
claims.inference: An explicit Three discriminator that now sits beside the adverse lines (C213, C214, C140) rather than without them (critic-05, enneagram-07).
claims.alternative: Public self-deprecation can itself be image management; the article concedes that Four-leaning-Three and Three-leaning-Four are not cleanly separable here (C229).

claims.claim: Interpretation: the dated printed statements (Vogue UK, January 2016; Vogue and Glamour UK, 2017) affirm pride and refuse to distance her from the films; neither denies that the production was contested. They show a promotional line held for years, not a false denial of the fight, and do not move the reading toward a Three’s image management or a loyal Six’s discipline on their own.
claims.passage: She stayed on message about _Fifty Shades_ for years
claims.inference: Holding back a grievance while promoting is common to every type under contract; what is type-relevant is that the feeling she stated (pride in something “different”) is the one she kept.
claims.alternative: If a dated statement in which she flatly denied any conflict surfaces, the Three or loyal-Six reading of those years strengthens.
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if a 2015–2021 statement denying the fight itself is found.

claims.claim: Interpretation: a collaborator’s account of a TeaTime production gone wrong could move the read; a fight framed as being misled or left unprotected points toward Six, one framed as the work made false toward Four.
claims.passage: If one does, its shape will matter: a fight framed as being misled or left unprotected would point toward Six, one framed as the work made false toward Four.
claims.inference: Names an observable reopen signal for the contested typing.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh, on the release of Three Incestuous Sisters, and whenever a non-promotional long-form account or collaborator testimony appears.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what she mourns at wrap is the connection to the material inside the safe set, and by her own account it has happened more times than she can count.
claims.passage: What she keeps losing, and keeps going back to build, is the connection inside it.
claims.inference: Vogue ties the grief to films with “this really intense connection to the material” (C116); “more times than she can count” paraphrases “I don’t even know how many times.”
claims.alternative: Common among actors; a Six could mourn the secure group itself (C118).

claims.claim: Dakota Johnson is an American actress (Wikipedia) and producer (TeaTime; AP, Vogue), best known for the Fifty Shades of Grey films (Wikipedia: her breakthrough; Vogue 2026: “shot her into the stratosphere”).
claims.passage: Dakota Johnson, the American actress and producer best known for the _Fifty Shades of Grey_ films
claims.inference: Orientation for a cold reader.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Of the three-picture contract she signed at 23, after James, by Johnson’s account, scrapped Patrick Marber’s script in anger over Charlie Hunnam’s exit, she told Vanity Fair in 2022, “I was young. I was 23. So it was scary,” then, “It just became something crazy,” she continued.
claims.passage: Of the three-picture contract she signed, with the script she had signed on for already gone: "I was young. I was 23. So it was scary."
claims.inference: The stated fear is of being bound by contract to a production that had changed under her; the article now states that context beside the quote (fan-02, critic-01). Vanity Fair, not Johnson, adds the Hitchcock-contract comparison, which is not used.
claims.alternative: A 23-year-old signing a three-picture contract would be scared regardless of type; Vanity Fair, not Johnson, links it to Hitchcock’s contract with her grandmother.

claims.claim: In 2022, answering rumors of a feud with Jamie Dornan (“There was never a time when we didn’t get along… he’s like a brother to me”), she said, “We had to really trust each other and protect each other.” Of the more outrageous scenes she said, “We were doing the weirdest things for years, and we needed to be a team: ‘We’re not doing that,’ or ‘You can’t do that camera angle.’” The article quotes the first line.
claims.passage: Of her costar Jamie Dornan: "We had to really trust each other and protect each other."
claims.inference: The protection is mutual and bodily, in explicit scenes; it is said in defense of the Dornan friendship, not as a complaint about an authority.
claims.alternative: The trust line answers rumors of a feud with Dornan; refusing camera angles is also ordinary boundary-setting on intimate scenes, and fits an expressive or Eight reading as well.

claims.claim: Interpretation: read alone, the 2022 fear and protection lines (C165, C166) are compatible with a Six’s story, and the fear is of being bound to a production that had changed after she committed; read in their own passage, where she adds that “both Jamie and I were treated really well” and that James “was always kind to me,” the complaint that survives is which movie got made.
claims.passage: Read alone, those lines tell a Six's story; the fear is of a production that had changed after she committed.
claims.inference: Concedes the counterevidence the verifier raised (verify-02) before weighing it.
claims.alternative: A Six can also say she was treated well and still feel unsafe; the counterweight is that in the interviews reviewed she has not named anyone who misled her or an unmet need for protection as the injury.

claims.claim: In the same 2022 passage she said, “There are things that I still cannot say because I don’t want to hurt anyone’s career and I don’t want to damage anybody’s reputation, but both Jamie and I were treated really well.”
claims.passage: "There are things that I still cannot say because I don't want to hurt anyone's career and I don't want to damage anybody's reputation, but both Jamie and I were treated really well."
claims.inference: She declines to frame the set as mistreatment of the two actors, and says she is still withholding details to protect others’ careers; this is why the limits paragraph (C94) keeps a suppressed trust grievance open.
claims.alternative: “Treated really well” is also what a promotionally careful or loyal speaker would say; the withheld details are unknown.

claims.claim: Interpretation: when she sums up her troubled films and the industry across 2020, 2024 and 2025, the complaint is lost expression and sameness: a film “comes out as a totally different thing” (2020); “no room for being expressive… It’s contrived” (2024); “Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring” (2024); Madame Web “turned into something else” and “creative decisions are made by committee” (2025); studios will not make what is “different or risky” (Cannes, 2025). The exception the article marks is the 2024 distrust line (C179).
claims.passage: Her industry critique keeps that shape, with one exception.
claims.inference: Repeats C75, C74 and C76 as a pattern across three outlets and five years.
claims.alternative: Expression vocabulary is industry-standard; all are promotional interviews.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Four reading leads on the content of her self-definition (difference, being seen, not belonging), on the content of her grievances (lost expression) and on what she adds when she overrides fear (a vision, a gaze she is shedding); the Six reading stays live on the volume of her fear and support language. The usable test is the target: a counterphobic Six aims defiance at the authority or the fear, a Four aims expression at the work and the self. “I just won’t let anybody else do it” reads either way; her grievances across 2020–2025 take the expression form.
claims.passage: So the usable test is narrower than temperature: a counterphobic Six aims defiance at the authority or the fear; a Four aims expression at the work and the self. "I just won't let anybody else do it" reads either way. Her grievances, across 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, take the second form.
claims.inference: Restated in terms the counterphobic variant predicts (enneagram-02, critic-03): rule and method refusals and the Bustle defiance line are no longer counted against Six, and the ally present in each override is conceded (C223, C224). The reason the call stays at medium confidence.
claims.alternative: A reader weighting her most detailed account (Vanity Fair 2022) over her summaries, or reading “I just won’t let anybody else do it” as refusal to cede, could favor Six.
claims.review_trigger: Check at each refresh whether new first-person accounts of fear credit trusted people and preparation (Six) or freedom to feel and express (Four).

claims.claim: Asked by Glamour UK in early 2017 whether she ever wished she hadn’t made the Fifty Shades films, she said, “It comes in waves,” and, in the same answer, “I do feel proud of it.”
claims.passage: Asked by Glamour UK that year whether she ever wished she hadn't made them: "It comes in waves," and, in the same answer, "I do feel proud of it."
claims.inference: During promotion she admitted recurring regret alongside pride, so the promotion years show withholding of the fight rather than a faked, unmixed feeling.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type Four and keeps Six alive. (1) Fear and anxiety recur across the whole record: fame “can completely destroy a human too” (2015, C186); “Whenever I have downtime, I’m unsure that I will ever work again” (2016, C177); “feeling so scared of people” after two years of exposure (2017, C35); “when I don’t feel protected, I tend to close right up” (2017, C20); stage fright and a panic attack when the cameras rolled on a singing scene (2021, C90); “this fear of when you have the potential to do things, but you’re just like, is that going to be okay?” and Gyllenhaal as her “shepherd” (2021, C45); “everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press” (2026, C91); “I don’t have the confidence” to direct (2025, C180). (2) Her safety and protection language is Six-shaped on its own: protection from collaborators who “give me a chance” precedes the freedom to act (C20, C150, C151); moviemaking “makes things feel a little bit more safe” (2022, C98); she trusted Gyllenhaal partly because “she knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care” (2021, C100); she builds “a protective maternal space” for people who have been “not taken care of or not seen on set” (2026, C26) and “can’t waste time on toxic sets anymore” (2025, C181); streaming bosses “don’t trust creative people or artists” (2024, C179). (3) Her fullest Fifty Shades account (2022) contains fear and mutual protection on a production that changed after she signed: the script she signed on for was scrapped (C209), the contract at 23 “was scary” (C165), she and Dornan “had to really trust each other and protect each other” (C166), and read as structure the passage is an authority with “creative control, all day, every day” resisted covertly and judged “psychotic” in hindsight (C220, C136). Her 2024 line about the author’s involvement, “It’s also about control and feeling powerful, and that’s not what art is,” is her one grievance in the shape of power (C79). (4) The Bustle defiance (“I am shaking, even if I had no interest”) reads counterphobic if taken literally, though she softened it lines later (C218) and flagged the interview as exaggerated (C22, C93, C129); her refusals of method and rules fit a counterphobic Six as well as a Four (C224). (5) Three: “this is a business” (C39); years on message for Fifty Shades (C156, C08, C171) with the 2022 account arriving when distancing cost least (C140); “It wasn’t my fault” (C213); self-deprecation and viral candor as image management (C214). (6) Two: womb-like sets, “protective maternal space,” porousness, protectiveness toward Burghardt (C193). (7) Eight for the Ellen correction, “takes no prisoners” and the control grievance (C09, C34, C79); Nine for days alone, “along for the ride,” “they don’t pour out of me” and accommodate-then-decide (C32, C106, C217, C218); Seven for play, press put-ons and comedy as a “lifelong tool” (C33, C11, C182). (8) Incentives and circumstance: “authentic,” “different” and “brave” are industry vocabulary; a rootless, tabloid-exposed childhood (C02, C03, C63) explains privacy, vigilance and not belonging without any type; lifelong depression (C04) can mimic Four melancholy and is not used as evidence; nearly all testimony is from friends and collaborators in promotional pieces, and the outside voices (S35, S38, S44, S51, S52) do not speak to motive (C113); the record was not exhausted (Good Hang with Amy Poehler, 2025-06-10, unopened).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Counterphobic Type Six is the strongest rival. The volume of fear language is the Six’s: doubt about being wanted or working again (C177), fear of people and of exposure (C35, C91, C186), stage fright (C90), the contract that “was scary” on a production that had changed under her (C165, C209), the question “is that going to be okay?” (C45) and the admitted lack of confidence to direct (C180). Her remedies are the Six’s too: a trusted guide (“shepherd,” C45; “such good hands,” C29), mutual protection (“protect each other,” C166), a protected set for people who were “not taken care of” (C26, C117, C82), a refusal of “toxic sets” (C181), rules for others while rejecting rules for herself (C13, C24, C224), and reflexive defiance of anyone who says she cannot (C22). Her Fifty Shades account can be read as an illegitimate authority resisted covertly (C220), her 2024 line as a grievance about “control and feeling powerful” (C79), and her industry critique as distrust (“don’t trust creative people or artists,” C179). On this reading, TeaTime is a security structure, the deadpan is vigilance (“a survival tactic,” C84) and the Four-sounding talk of difference is the counterphobic Six’s refusal to be told what to do. Type Three is the second rival (commercial frankness, years on message, timing of grievances, “It wasn’t my fault,” bankable candor: C39, C156, C140, C213, C214) and is conceded as not cleanly separable from a Four leaning toward Three (C229). Type Two (C193), Eight (C09, C34, C79), Nine (C32, C106, C217, C218, C219) and Seven (C11, C33, C182) each explain a visible piece and fail on her standing intensity of feeling (C18), her appetite for “the pain and the suffering” (C44), her repeated self-definition by difference and not belonging (C06, C08, C179, C215, C216) and what she does when peace would be easier (C227).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: The relation between her fear and her grievance (C95, C184, C190), stated as this profile’s reading of the interviews reviewed (2015–2026) and tested against the strongest Six evidence rather than around it. She names fear freely, and every fear named in this record is circumstantial: fame (2015, 2017), the three-picture contract at 23 (2022), singing (2021), directing (2025), press scrutiny (2026), not working (2016). The test for a Six is whether fear and grievance fuse in one figure: an authority who misled her, left her exposed, or imposed its will without the right to; the Four’s grievance is the loss of what was true in the work. In the one passage where fear and grievance meet (Vanity Fair, 2022) the fear attaches to a contract on a production that had already changed under her (C165, C209), the praise to James and to how she and Dornan were treated (C168, C71), and the complaint to which movie got made (C69, C184). Read as structure, the same passage is a counterphobic Six’s story: an author with control “all day, every day” resisted covertly and judged “psychotic” (C220). What tips it toward Four is narrow and is stated as such: she never disputes James’s right to the control she held and is “grateful she wanted me to be in those movies” (C71); she answers “Combo” and spreads the blame across studio, directors and author (C211); and the wrong she names in 2022 and 2024 is what the control did to the work, “contrived,” “that’s not what art is,” not what it did to her (C74, C79, C210). Taylor-Johnson’s and James’s accounts establish only that the first film’s fight was real and two-sided (C221). The protection-shaped lines in the record are carried, not omitted: “not handled with grace and with care” (C100), “not taken care of or not seen” (C26), “toxic sets” (C181), “don’t trust creative people or artists” (C179); what keeps Four ahead is the object of each: care for people’s freedom to express themselves, a toxic set defined by unkindness rather than betrayal, distrust of artists (C222). Across outlets and years the grievance keeps the expression shape: a film “comes out as a totally different thing” (2020, C75); “no room for being expressive… It’s contrived” (2024, C74); “the safe thing is really boring” (2024, C30); Madame Web “turned into something else” and decisions “made by committee” (2025, C76, C213); studios will not make what is “different or risky” (2025, C187). Her self-definition has the same content: “different is what I’m about” (2017, C08), Fincher’s “did something different” (2022, C06), “to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach” and “deeper and darker, more real and more honest” (2021, C16, C192), “I just want to be authentic” when called cool (2026, C14, C53), and the Four’s harder core in plainer words: “I don’t know if I’m from anywhere or I belong anywhere” (2024, C215) and “there was something wrong with my brain. Now I realize that it just works in a different way” (2017, C216). When she overrides fear the override is mixed: a trusted person and a vision claim arrive in the same answer (C190, C223), so the tilt rests on what she adds, not on the absence of allies; rule and method refusals fit the counterphobic Six as well (C224). The usable test is therefore the target: a counterphobic Six aims defiance at the authority or the fear, a Four aims expression at the work and the self; “I just won’t let anybody else do it” reads either way; her grievances across 2020–2025 take the expression form (C170). Against Three: timing, “It wasn’t my fault” and bankable candor are conceded (C140, C213, C214); she shrugs at flops (C111), says she doesn’t “make sense” in the superhero world (C28), would accept a small film as her last (C82), and aims grievances at contrivance rather than reception (C155); Four-leaning-Three and Three-leaning-Four are not cleanly separable here (C229). Against Two: she never locates her worth in being needed (C193). Against Eight: volunteered fear and tenderness (C35, C103) and ceded control to a trusted filmmaker (C29). Against Nine: standing intensity (C18), the on-air correction, the ruffled feathers and the fight she picked (C227), with the Nine-shaped lines on the page (C217, C218, C219). Against Seven: the appetite explicitly includes “the pain and the suffering” (C44) and comedy is her way to “look it in the eyes” (C182). Limits: the discriminator rests on self-report in promotional settings, on her own account of a dispute whose other party has not answered (C70), on content she has incentives to frame as artistic, and on an unexhausted record; the Six reading is not refuted, only outweighed on content, and the lead narrows once the protection-shaped lines are counted. Hence medium confidence.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why the fear is so loud for a Four: anxiety and self-doubt run through every decade (C177, C45, C90, C91, C112), and a Four-with-Six-cover and a Six-with-Four-cover remain distinguishable only by content, not by temperature. The Fifty Shades promotional years: dated statements of pride (2016, 2017: C156, C08, C171) followed by the 2022 account she said she could not give “truthfully” before (C67); read here as withholding the fight, not inventing a feeling (C148, C175), but a Three’s discipline is not excluded (C140, C214, C229). The Easter Bunny line, in which movies serve safety (C98). The “control and feeling powerful” line, her one grievance in the shape of power (C79, C210). Her relish for put-ons (“The most fun,” the shifting limes confession) in someone who says “It’s hard for me to fake it” (C11, C15, C52). The Madame Web reversal between 2024 and 2025 (C28, C111). The slapstick, costume-party sociability friends describe (C33). Whether the defiance is temperament or a learned response to a childhood in the tabloids (C63). Wing and instinctual subtype are not established.
